title: Blocks of Filled Cells After Each Addition

concept.title: Store the block length at both ends of every block, so a new cell can join its neighbours in constant time
body: A row has `L` cells, all empty at first. Cells are filled one at a time. A *block* is a maximal group of neighbouring filled cells. After **every** filling, print how many blocks there are and how long the **longest** block is. For `L = 10` and the cells `5 2 4 3 3` the blocks are: after `5`: 1 block, longest 1; after `2`: 2 blocks, longest 1; after `4`: 2 blocks (`2` and `4-5`), longest 2; after `3`: 1 block `2-5`, longest 4; after the second `3`: nothing changes.

Let `length[x]` be the length of the block when `x` is one of its two **end** cells. When a new cell `x` is filled, its left neighbour `x-1` (if filled) is the right end of a block of length `left = length[x-1]`, and `x+1` is the left end of a block of length `right = length[x+1]`; both are 0 if the cell is empty. The new block has the length `total = left + right + 1`, and it begins at `x - left` and ends at `x + right`. We write `total` into **both** of these end cells (and into `x`). The number of blocks changes by `1 - (left > 0) - (right > 0)`: a new block appears, and each existing neighbour block disappears into it.

body.code:
length = [0] * (L + 2)
blocks = longest = 0
for x in cells:
    if length[x] == 0:                      # a new cell
        left, right = length[x - 1], length[x + 1]
        total = left + right + 1
        length[x - left] = length[x + right] = length[x] = total
        blocks += 1 - (left > 0) - (right > 0)
        longest = max(longest, total)
    # print blocks and longest after this step

body: Values inside a block may be out of date, but they are never read: we only read the cells next to the new cell, and those are always block ends with correct values. An already filled cell has `length[x] > 0`, so repeated additions are ignored. Each addition costs O(1). (A union-find structure with sizes gives the same answers in almost O(1).)

statement: A row of `L` empty cells is given, and `q` cells are filled one after another (a cell can be filled again, which changes nothing). After each filling print the number of blocks of consecutive filled cells and the length of the longest block. Print two lines: the first has the `q` numbers of blocks, the second has the `q` longest lengths.
inputFormat: The first line has `L` and `q`: the number of cells in a row and the number of additions.
The second line has `q` numbers: the cells that are filled one by one (a cell may be filled more than once).
outputFormat: The first line has `q` numbers: the number of blocks after each filling.
The second line has `q` numbers: the length of the longest block after each filling.
hints: A new cell can merge up to two blocks.
Keep the block length at the ends of each block.
The number of blocks changes by 1 minus the number of neighbouring filled cells.

input = sys.stdin.readline

L, q = map(int, input().split())

explanation: The length of every block is stored at both of its end cells; a new cell reads the lengths of its two neighbours, writes the merged length at the new ends, and updates the number of blocks and the longest length.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

L, q = map(int, input().split())
cells = list(map(int, input().split()))

length = [0] * (L + 2)
blocks = longest = 0
blocks_out = []
longest_out = []
for x in cells:
    if length[x] == 0:
        left = length[x - 1]
        right = length[x + 1]
        total = left + right + 1
        length[x - left] = total
        length[x + right] = total
        length[x] = total
        blocks += 1 - (1 if left > 0 else 0) - (1 if right > 0 else 0)
        if total > longest:
            longest = total
    blocks_out.append(blocks)
    longest_out.append(longest)
print(*blocks_out)
print(*longest_out)
